title: Set Difference
story: Your friend has a list of movies they've seen. You have your own list. You want to find: 'What movies have I seen that my friend hasn't?' In set theory, this is called the difference — A minus B. Let's compute it!
why: Set operations — difference, intersection, union — are essential for comparing collections, finding unique items, and answering 'what's missing?' questions across any domain.
analogy: Set difference is like two playlists: your playlist minus your friend's playlist = songs only YOU have. It's the musical equivalent of 'what do I know that you don't?' Intersection is 'what do we both know?'
try_it: Write `set_union` that returns all items that appear in EITHER set (no duplicates). Then write `set_symmetric_difference` — items that are in exactly one set but NOT both (A xor B). Build a function `jaccard_similarity` that computes |intersection| / |union| — the standard measure of how similar two sets are (0.0 = nothing in common, 1.0 = identical).
tips: Difference uses `!b.contains(x)` — the NOT is the key difference from intersection
Always iterate over the Vec of keys, not the Set — Set has no guaranteed iteration order
For union, iterate over items from BOTH sets and use a result Set to prevent duplicates
common_mistakes: Computing difference by checking `a.contains` against `b` — difference should check `b.contains`, using `a` as the source
Forgetting the `!` in difference — without it, you get intersection instead
Iterating over a Set directly (if possible) — the iteration order is unpredictable; use a Vec for ordering
